architectural_implications.after: A separate evaluator agent navigates the artifact (e.g., Playwright), scores against an explicit rubric, and returns structured critique to the generator.
architectural_implications.before: A single agent generates output and self-reviews it in the same context window.
architectural_implications.consequence: Verification becomes independently tunable and auditable, but introduces additional inference cost and a new tuning burden (making the evaluator appropriately harsh).
architectural_implications.observation: Verification is moved out of the generating context into a dedicated adversarial evaluator agent with its own tooling and rubrics.

architectural_implications.after: Planner, Generator, and Evaluator run with zero shared context and exchange specs, sprint contracts, and state via files.
architectural_implications.before: Multiple roles share one accumulating context and implicit conversational state.
architectural_implications.consequence: Context rot is avoided and every inter-agent agreement becomes a durable artifact, but the harness now needs file schemas, contract negotiation steps, and tooling to inspect the resulting state.
architectural_implications.observation: Coordination substrate shifts from the shared context window to concrete files on disk.

architectural_implications.after: Scaffolding is deleted when a model upgrade absorbs the capability (e.g., context resets and sprint decomposition dropped between Opus 4.5 and 4.6).
architectural_implications.before: Orchestration scaffolding accumulates over time to compensate for model weaknesses.
architectural_implications.consequence: Harness architecture must be re-validated on every model upgrade, adding a recurring migration cost but preventing stale complexity from degrading performance.
architectural_implications.observation: Harness layers are treated as removable rather than permanent.

architectural_implications.after: A Planner converts a one-line prompt into a high-level spec and sprint workflow that downstream agents follow.
architectural_implications.before: The harness hard-codes sprint structure and planning steps in its control flow.
architectural_implications.consequence: Planning becomes prompt- and model-mediated (and therefore improvable with model upgrades) rather than an invariant of the orchestration code.
architectural_implications.observation: Task decomposition is delegated to a Planner agent instead of being fixed in the harness.

source.title: Anthropic Workshop: Build Agents That Run for Hours — Ash Prabaker & Andrew Wilson

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Ash Prabaker and Andrew Wilson
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Building and maintaining long-running AI agents using Claude models and custom agent harnesses
  • Purpose: To educate AI engineers on the architectural patterns, harnesses, and model evolutions required to successfully run coding and development agents autonomously for extended periods (5 to 30+ hours). Ash Prabaker and Andrew Wilson from Anthropic's Applied AI team discuss the evolution of Claude models and agent harnesses over a year, focusing on how to build agents that can run for hours without losing coherence, planning, or quality. They examine the three reasons agents lose the plot—context degradation, planning failures, and poor self-verification—and present practical fixes including model capability improvements, harness design patterns like the generator-evaluator loop (inspired by GANs), sprint contracts, and file system sharing.

Topic Map

Introduction and Problem Framing

  • Explanation: Introduces the speakers from Anthropic and frames the core challenge: building agents that can run for hours on complex tasks without losing context or intent.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents running for 5 to 6+ hours require careful harness design, not just one-shot model prompting.
    • Demos of one-shot browser execution often hide the underlying complexity of the agent harness.
  • Examples:
    • One-shot browser demos vs. multi-hour agent harnesses.
  • Terminology:
    • agent harness
    • applied AI
    • context management
  • Why it matters: Setting expectations for production agent deployments beyond short prompt-response cycles.

Three Reasons Agents Lose the Plot

  • Explanation: Analyzes why long-running agents fail, categorizing failures into context limits, planning deficiencies, and poor self-verification.
  • Key claims:
    • Context windows are finite and suffer from coherence degradation as sessions deepen.
    • Models struggle with long-term planning, often trying to one-shot tasks or stopping prematurely.
    • Models are poor judges of their own code output, exhibiting sycophancy and superficial testing.
  • Examples:
    • Curl testing instead of click testing in browser apps.
    • Stubs features and moving on without checking backend implementation.
  • Terminology:
    • context rot
    • context anxiety
    • reward hacking
    • sycophancy
  • Why it matters: Identifies the core failure modes engineers must engineer around when building autonomous agents.

Evolution of Claude Models and Harnesses

  • Explanation: Walks through a timeline from Sonnet 3.5 to Opus 4.6, demonstrating how models and harnesses co-evolved to extend autonomous runtime from minutes to days.
  • Key claims:
    • Model task completion horizons increased from 1 hour (Sonnet 3.7) to 12+ hours (Opus 4.6).
    • Harnesses have co-evolved with models, starting with complex multi-prompt loops and shedding unnecessary scaffolding as models became more capable.
  • Examples:
    • Artifacts introduced in Sonnet 3.5 providing the first closed feedback loop.
    • Claude Code and agent SDK releases featuring checkpoints, memory tools, and agent teams.
  • Terminology:
    • METR Horizon
    • Claude Code
    • MCP servers
    • agent SDK
    • agent teams
  • Why it matters: Shows the trajectory of LLM agent capability and how hardware/model upgrades shift the burden from harness complexity to model intelligence.

Harness Design: Separating Builder from Judge

  • Explanation: Presents the generator-evaluator loop inspired by GANs, where a separate evaluator agent (using Playwright and rubrics) tests and critiques the generator's work.
  • Key claims:
    • Tuning a standalone evaluator to be skeptical and harsh is tractable; making a generator self-critical is not.
    • Subjective quality like design and originality can be graded using detailed rubrics applied by an adversarial evaluator.
  • Examples:
    • Frontend web development loop where Playwright navigates, scores, and critiques pages before passing feedback to the generator.
  • Terminology:
    • generator-evaluator loop
    • adversarial evaluator
    • Playwright
    • subjective quality gradable
  • Why it matters: Solves the self-evaluation flaw in LLMs by introducing an adversarial feedback loop.

Scaling to Full Stack with Three Agents

  • Explanation: Introduces a three-agent architecture—Planner, Generator, and Evaluator—communicating exclusively via the filesystem.
  • Key claims:
    • A Planner agent breaks a high-level 1-line prompt into a high-level spec and sprint workflow.
    • Generator and Evaluator negotiate sprint contracts via files before writing any code.
    • Zero shared context; all coordination goes through files on disk to prevent context rot.
  • Examples:
    • Retro game maker and browser music production app built over 4 to 6 hours using the 3-agent harness.
  • Terminology:
    • Planner agent
    • Generator agent
    • Evaluator agent
    • sprint contracts
    • filesystem state
  • Why it matters: Provides a robust, production-tested blueprint for multi-hour autonomous software engineering agents.

Key Points

Self-evaluation is a trap

  • Explanation: LLMs cannot reliably evaluate their own work objectively due to sycophancy and bias toward finishing tasks.
  • Evidence: Out of the box, Claude identifies legitimate issues but talks itself into approving flawed work anyway.
  • Practical implication: Always separate the builder from the judge by using an independent adversarial evaluator agent.

Compaction doesn't cure coherence drift

  • Explanation: Summarizing or compacting long session contexts leads to loss of detail and drifting off task.
  • Evidence: Long-running sessions degrade in coherence as context windows fill up.
  • Practical implication: Use structured handoffs, fresh context windows per session, and filesystem artifacts for state persistence.

Make subjective quality gradable

  • Explanation: Quality metrics like design taste and originality can be evaluated deterministically if broken down into explicit rubrics.
  • Evidence: Using a 4-criteria rubric (design, originality, craft, functionality) paired with Playwright navigation successfully prevented purple-gradient slop.
  • Practical implication: Write detailed rubrics for your evaluator agent rather than relying on vague prompts.

Read the traces

  • Explanation: Debugging long-running agents requires analyzing step-by-step logs rather than guessing at prompt failures.
  • Evidence: The primary debugging loop is reading evaluator logs, finding where judgment diverged, and updating prompts.
  • Practical implication: Build tooling to inspect agent transcripts and trace execution history.

Harnesses are on a diet as models improve

  • Explanation: As base models become more capable and context-aware, complex scaffolding can be removed.
  • Evidence: Moving from Opus 4.5 to 4.6 dropped context resets between sessions, sprint decomposition, and per-sprint evaluator cadence in favor of continuous builds.
  • Practical implication: Continuously re-evaluate your harness architecture as newer, smarter models are released.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Generator-Evaluator Loop

  • How it works: A generator model builds an artifact, and an independent evaluator model tests and grades it against explicit criteria, feeding actionable critique back into the loop.
  • Components:
    • Generator (builds the thing)
    • Evaluator (grades the thing using tools like Playwright and rubrics)
    • Feedback channel (critique and refinement)
  • When to use: When building multi-hour autonomous coding or creative agents where self-verification is critical.

Three-Agent Full Stack Architecture

  • How it works: Splits tasks across three distinct agents—Planner, Generator, and Evaluator—coordinating via local files on disk with zero shared context.
  • Components:
    • Planner (breaks 1-line prompt into spec and sprint milestones)
    • Generator (executes one sprint at a time)
    • Evaluator (tests against contract via Playwright and rubric)
    • Filesystem (shared state via spec.md, app/git, findings.md)
  • When to use: For building complex, full-stack software applications autonomously over several hours.

Examples & Case Studies

Building a retro game maker and a browser Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) using solo agents vs. full multi-agent harnesses.

  • Illustrates: Solo agents failed at play mode and sprite interaction after 20 minutes, whereas the 3-agent harness successfully built fully featured, tested apps over 6 hours.
  • Lesson: Complex multi-hour tasks require structured planning, sprint contracts, and adversarial evaluation.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Use separate adversarial evaluator agents instead of letting models grade their own work.
    • Rely on filesystem state (spec.md, progress.md) instead of infinite context windows for long tasks.
    • Break subjective quality into explicit rubrics for automated evaluation tools like Playwright.
  • Strategic:
    • Harness design co-evolves with base model capabilities; be ready to strip out scaffolding as models improve.
    • Granular contract criteria (e.g., 27 specific criteria per sprint) prevent vague agent outputs.
    • Treat prompt engineering for agents like writing rigorous software specifications.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How to scale multi-agent team communication without excessive API costs?

## Overview
- **Speaker**: Ash Prabaker and Andrew Wilson
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Building and maintaining long-running AI agents using Claude models and custom agent harnesses
- **Purpose**: To educate AI engineers on the architectural patterns, harnesses, and model evolutions required to successfully run coding and development agents autonomously for extended periods (5 to 30+ hours).
Ash Prabaker and Andrew Wilson from Anthropic's Applied AI team discuss the evolution of Claude models and agent harnesses over a year, focusing on how to build agents that can run for hours without losing coherence, planning, or quality. They examine the three reasons agents lose the plot—context degradation, planning failures, and poor self-verification—and present practical fixes including model capability improvements, harness design patterns like the generator-evaluator loop (inspired by GANs), sprint contracts, and file system sharing.
## Topic Map
### Introduction and Problem Framing
- **Explanation**: Introduces the speakers from Anthropic and frames the core challenge: building agents that can run for hours on complex tasks without losing context or intent.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents running for 5 to 6+ hours require careful harness design, not just one-shot model prompting.
  - Demos of one-shot browser execution often hide the underlying complexity of the agent harness.
- **Examples**:
  - One-shot browser demos vs. multi-hour agent harnesses.
- **Terminology**:
  - agent harness
  - applied AI
  - context management
- **Why it matters**: Setting expectations for production agent deployments beyond short prompt-response cycles.
### Three Reasons Agents Lose the Plot
- **Explanation**: Analyzes why long-running agents fail, categorizing failures into context limits, planning deficiencies, and poor self-verification.
- **Key claims**:
  - Context windows are finite and suffer from coherence degradation as sessions deepen.
  - Models struggle with long-term planning, often trying to one-shot tasks or stopping prematurely.
  - Models are poor judges of their own code output, exhibiting sycophancy and superficial testing.
- **Examples**:
  - Curl testing instead of click testing in browser apps.
  - Stubs features and moving on without checking backend implementation.
- **Terminology**:
  - context rot
  - context anxiety
  - reward hacking
  - sycophancy
- **Why it matters**: Identifies the core failure modes engineers must engineer around when building autonomous agents.
### Evolution of Claude Models and Harnesses
- **Explanation**: Walks through a timeline from Sonnet 3.5 to Opus 4.6, demonstrating how models and harnesses co-evolved to extend autonomous runtime from minutes to days.
- **Key claims**:
  - Model task completion horizons increased from 1 hour (Sonnet 3.7) to 12+ hours (Opus 4.6).
  - Harnesses have co-evolved with models, starting with complex multi-prompt loops and shedding unnecessary scaffolding as models became more capable.
- **Examples**:
  - Artifacts introduced in Sonnet 3.5 providing the first closed feedback loop.
  - Claude Code and agent SDK releases featuring checkpoints, memory tools, and agent teams.
- **Terminology**:
  - METR Horizon
  - Claude Code
  - MCP servers
  - agent SDK
  - agent teams
- **Why it matters**: Shows the trajectory of LLM agent capability and how hardware/model upgrades shift the burden from harness complexity to model intelligence.
### Harness Design: Separating Builder from Judge
- **Explanation**: Presents the generator-evaluator loop inspired by GANs, where a separate evaluator agent (using Playwright and rubrics) tests and critiques the generator's work.
- **Key claims**:
  - Tuning a standalone evaluator to be skeptical and harsh is tractable; making a generator self-critical is not.
  - Subjective quality like design and originality can be graded using detailed rubrics applied by an adversarial evaluator.
- **Examples**:
  - Frontend web development loop where Playwright navigates, scores, and critiques pages before passing feedback to the generator.
- **Terminology**:
  - generator-evaluator loop
  - adversarial evaluator
  - Playwright
  - subjective quality gradable
- **Why it matters**: Solves the self-evaluation flaw in LLMs by introducing an adversarial feedback loop.
### Scaling to Full Stack with Three Agents
- **Explanation**: Introduces a three-agent architecture—Planner, Generator, and Evaluator—communicating exclusively via the filesystem.
- **Key claims**:
  - A Planner agent breaks a high-level 1-line prompt into a high-level spec and sprint workflow.
  - Generator and Evaluator negotiate sprint contracts via files before writing any code.
  - Zero shared context; all coordination goes through files on disk to prevent context rot.
- **Examples**:
  - Retro game maker and browser music production app built over 4 to 6 hours using the 3-agent harness.
- **Terminology**:
  - Planner agent
  - Generator agent
  - Evaluator agent
  - sprint contracts
  - filesystem state
- **Why it matters**: Provides a robust, production-tested blueprint for multi-hour autonomous software engineering agents.
## Key Points
### Self-evaluation is a trap
- **Explanation**: LLMs cannot reliably evaluate their own work objectively due to sycophancy and bias toward finishing tasks.
- **Evidence**: Out of the box, Claude identifies legitimate issues but talks itself into approving flawed work anyway.
- **Practical implication**: Always separate the builder from the judge by using an independent adversarial evaluator agent.
### Compaction doesn't cure coherence drift
- **Explanation**: Summarizing or compacting long session contexts leads to loss of detail and drifting off task.
- **Evidence**: Long-running sessions degrade in coherence as context windows fill up.
- **Practical implication**: Use structured handoffs, fresh context windows per session, and filesystem artifacts for state persistence.
### Make subjective quality gradable
- **Explanation**: Quality metrics like design taste and originality can be evaluated deterministically if broken down into explicit rubrics.
- **Evidence**: Using a 4-criteria rubric (design, originality, craft, functionality) paired with Playwright navigation successfully prevented purple-gradient slop.
- **Practical implication**: Write detailed rubrics for your evaluator agent rather than relying on vague prompts.
### Read the traces
- **Explanation**: Debugging long-running agents requires analyzing step-by-step logs rather than guessing at prompt failures.
- **Evidence**: The primary debugging loop is reading evaluator logs, finding where judgment diverged, and updating prompts.
- **Practical implication**: Build tooling to inspect agent transcripts and trace execution history.
### Harnesses are on a diet as models improve
- **Explanation**: As base models become more capable and context-aware, complex scaffolding can be removed.
- **Evidence**: Moving from Opus 4.5 to 4.6 dropped context resets between sessions, sprint decomposition, and per-sprint evaluator cadence in favor of continuous builds.
- **Practical implication**: Continuously re-evaluate your harness architecture as newer, smarter models are released.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Generator-Evaluator Loop
- **How it works**: A generator model builds an artifact, and an independent evaluator model tests and grades it against explicit criteria, feeding actionable critique back into the loop.
- **Components**:
  - Generator (builds the thing)
  - Evaluator (grades the thing using tools like Playwright and rubrics)
  - Feedback channel (critique and refinement)
- **When to use**: When building multi-hour autonomous coding or creative agents where self-verification is critical.
### Three-Agent Full Stack Architecture
- **How it works**: Splits tasks across three distinct agents—Planner, Generator, and Evaluator—coordinating via local files on disk with zero shared context.
- **Components**:
  - Planner (breaks 1-line prompt into spec and sprint milestones)
  - Generator (executes one sprint at a time)
  - Evaluator (tests against contract via Playwright and rubric)
  - Filesystem (shared state via spec.md, app/git, findings.md)
- **When to use**: For building complex, full-stack software applications autonomously over several hours.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Building a retro game maker and a browser Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) using solo agents vs. full multi-agent harnesses.
- **Illustrates**: Solo agents failed at play mode and sprite interaction after 20 minutes, whereas the 3-agent harness successfully built fully featured, tested apps over 6 hours.
- **Lesson**: Complex multi-hour tasks require structured planning, sprint contracts, and adversarial evaluation.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Use separate adversarial evaluator agents instead of letting models grade their own work.
  - Rely on filesystem state (spec.md, progress.md) instead of infinite context windows for long tasks.
  - Break subjective quality into explicit rubrics for automated evaluation tools like Playwright.
- **Strategic**:
  - Harness design co-evolves with base model capabilities; be ready to strip out scaffolding as models improve.
  - Granular contract criteria (e.g., 27 specific criteria per sprint) prevent vague agent outputs.
  - Treat prompt engineering for agents like writing rigorous software specifications.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How to scale multi-agent team communication without excessive API costs?
  - What are the optimal compaction strategies for long-running sessions in non-coding domains?
  - How to train models natively to be self-critical without requiring heavy external harnesses?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Tuning a standalone evaluator to be skeptical is tractable, but making a generator self-critical is not. (empirical observation)
- Models exhibit context anxiety and rush to finish tasks as they approach the end of their context window. (behavioral observation)
## Notable Quotes
> "The space of interesting harness combinations doesn't shrink as models improve. It moves." (at 27:22)
> "Out of the box, Claude is a poor QA agent. It would identify legitimate issues, then talk itself into deciding they weren't a big deal and approve the work anyway." (at 53:59)
> "Then Opus 4.6 shipped — and half of what we just showed you became dead weight." (at 56:55)
## Compressed Summary
- Self-evaluation in LLM agents fails due to sycophancy; adversarial evaluators are required.
- Context rot requires structured filesystem handoffs and fresh sessions rather than pure compaction.
- A three-agent architecture (Planner, Generator, Evaluator) successfully powers multi-hour autonomous software development.
- As base models improve with native context awareness and reasoning, harness scaffolding shrinks and simplifies.
